This page corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 29-1229.02 occupation "Hospitalists" (hospitalists): providing inpatient care predominantly in settings such as medical wards, acute care units, intensive care units, rehabilitation centers, or emergency rooms, and managing and coordinating patient care throughout treatment. Official scope text: Provide inpatient care predominantly in settings such as medical wards, acute care units, intensive care units, rehabilitation centers, or emergency rooms. Manage and coordinate patient care throughout treatment. The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET, and O*NET labels both datasets as the Physicians, All Other combined scope; the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; the two jurisdictions and their practice systems must not be applied to one another.

To judge whether hospital medicine suits you, first run one verifiable clinical drill using public or simulated materials: choose a fictional inpatient scenario (for example, admission for community-acquired pneumonia), and write a step-by-step process from receiving and admitting the patient, history taking and physical examination, ordering and interpreting laboratory and imaging studies, developing and placing the treatment plan, daily rounds and reassessment, multidisciplinary communication and coordination, to developing the discharge plan, writing the discharge summary, and handing over to the primary care physician, marking the basis for each judgment and the conditions requiring escalation or consultation, and the possible abnormalities (deterioration, adverse drug reactions, critical laboratory values, infection control events, failed post-discharge handoff). Afterward, check: whether recognizing and handling critical values and deterioration are treated as non-omittable items; whether matters beyond your individual authority or ability are written as consulting a supervising physician or initiating a consultation; and whether the basis for each judgment and the communication are written as reviewable records. Test with a real deliverable, not just answers to an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | The work activity importance ratings for U.S. O*NET 29-1229.02 show that assisting and caring for others (96), documenting/recording information (95), getting information (95), making decisions and solving problems (95), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (94), processing information (93), and analyzing data or information (91) are the most important activities for this occupation; work context shows that face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams 100% report every day, telephone conversations 100% report every day, frequency of decision making 92% report every day, indoors, environmentally controlled 96% report every day, contact with others 88%, typical work week 92% report more than 40 hours, exposure to disease or infections 88% report every day, work with a group or team 76% report extremely important, freedom to make decisions 71% report a lot of freedom, importance of being exact or accurate 60% report extremely important, and consequence of error 79% report extremely serious. The most important skills are active learning, active listening, critical thinking, reading comprehension, and speaking (all 78). If you are willing to work intensively with teams on the wards, make and re-check clinical judgments with incomplete information, and carry high-consequence responsibility, these daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (29-1229.02): typical work week 92% report more than 40 hours, consequence of error 79% report extremely serious, impact of decisions on co-workers or organizational outcomes 75% report very important results, work with a group or team 76% report extremely important, time pressure (strict deadlines) 60% report every day, physical proximity 63% report very close, and exposure to disease or infections 88% report every day. This occupation deals with inpatient diagnostic and treatment decisions, multidisciplinary collaboration, and high-consequence responsibility: a single missed critical value, a single misjudged medication or treatment decision, or a single lapse in handover or discharge coordination can cause patient harm and practice risk. This page therefore lists recognizing critical values and condition changes, verifying medication and treatment, handover and records, and consultation and escalation boundaries separately. On the U.S. side, this occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook, and the O*NET summary shows the combined scope related to 29-1229.02 is projected to grow at the average level (3%) from 2024 to 2034, with about 9,600 job openings per year and employment of about 340,700 in 2024, but those data are the Physicians, All Other combined scope and do not equal this occupation's precise size. If it is hard for you to sustain long, intense shifts, high-consequence decisions, and infection exposure, you should treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Commitment judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things within the same shift at once: make the clinical work solid (completing diagnosis and treatment based on history, examination, and tests, producing reviewable progress notes, orders, and discharge summaries); keep safety and boundaries under control (recognizing and escalating critical values and condition changes, verifying medication and procedures, handover and infection control, acting per institutional and regulatory requirements, and consulting or escalating when beyond your ability or authority); and carry definable position responsibility (be responsible for your own clinical judgments and records, and submit high-risk decisions to a supervising physician or team decision under institutional rules). It is recommended to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a step-by-step care process and progress notes, or a drill on recognizing and handling common inpatient situations), rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

The daily work of hospitalists can be broken down along three lines: (1) care and decisions—receiving and admitting patients, history and physical examination, ordering and interpreting tests, developing and adjusting treatment plans, and continuously assessing the condition; (2) coordination and continuity of care—communicating with the nursing team, specialty consultants, social service agencies, and the patient's primary care physician to maintain continuity; (3) records and handover—recording the course, orders, and communication points in written or electronic form, and completing handover and discharge summaries. The three lines share the same set of judgment and verification requirements, but their deliverables go to different recipients: care and decisions serve the patient directly, coordination serves the multidisciplinary team and primary care physicians, and records serve the reviewable medical record and the chain of responsibility.

paragraphs: Qualification boundaries (one) | Education, standardized training, practice registration, position authorization, and prescribing or signing authority are different states: completing education and training is not the same as obtaining practice registration, and obtaining registration is not the same as obtaining the institution's specific authorization for prescribing, procedures, and high-risk decisions.

Hospitalist is a U.S. physician role centered on inpatient care and coordination and is not equivalent to the Chinese professional title of resident physician or the standardized residency training stage. subject.name: Hospitalists
subject.summary: Hospitalists corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 29-1229.02 occupation "Hospitalists": providing inpatient care predominantly in settings such as medical wards, acute care units, intensive care units, rehabilitation centers, or emergency rooms, and managing and coordinating patient care throughout treatment. Official scope text: Provide inpatient care predominantly in settings such as medical wards, acute care units, intensive care units, rehabilitation centers, or emergency rooms. Manage and coordinate patient care throughout treatment. Core tasks include diagnosing, treating, or providing ongoing care (98), prescribing medication or treatment plans (98), ordering or interpreting tests such as laboratory work and X-rays (97), admitting patients to the hospital (96), and developing discharge plans and discharging patients (95). The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET, and O*NET labels both datasets as the Physicians, All Other combined scope; the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; China's physician practice and medical quality institutional boundaries are labeled separately.
